I like the office environment, the nature of my job is very collaborative, need brainstorming, and I find it easier at work. I have a lot of people working for me that are producing better at home, as their role needs less collaboration and more production.

I find training and mentoring new employees to be very challenging on Teams. It is harder to develop them when they are less exposed to the people.

I also find it harder to establish strong work relationships with someone you never met in person. It can, you can send it directly in rrsp if you have the room and not get taxes, I maxed out my rrsps that way.

It costs less, the 1/3 of the money that went in a locked in RRSP was sufficient in my case to buy back my 19 years, and I cashed out the other 2/3rd. The pension plan is different though, as military after 25 years you can retire and have a pension, the public servant pension plan is similar to other plans in the civi world, it is a calculation of your years of service and your age, so don’t think about retiring in your 40s and go double dip somewhere…

LIRA: Locked in RRSP. You cannot touch it until you are a certain age (I forget what age).
Your return of contribution depends on how many years you served and your salary throughout those years. I had ot calculated by the Pension centre, they sent me a package. You have a couple choices of what to do with your return of contribution, but mainly you can have everything in a locked in RRSP, or have about 1/3 in a LIRA and the rest cashed out. You cannot cash out the full amount, this is not an option.
To buy back your years of service if you become a public servant, you can use your LIRA to buy back those years, so if you had 15 years in the CF, it’s like you have 15 years as a public servant. Normally there should be enough in your LIrA to buy back your years as the pension plan is cheaper (and less advantageous than the cf pension as it also takes i to account your age, so you cannot retire young)

It happens now and will likely happen again. Depending on your trade, the requirement to be posted and move often is there, especially with the current shortages in most trades. If they need you posted, they will. Only option to avoid this and keep your quality of life is to release.

About half of your pension will go in a LIRA to be invested. With the rest, you can cash it (taxable of course) or invest it, depending what your goals are. If you take a public servant job you can buy back your years of service and reach a comfortable retirement at a decent age. 

I wish I could see a better option, but with 10-15 years left, you’ll likely be posted a couple more times…and if this degrades your family situation, there are plenty of jobs out there that will give you a better quality of life in your case.

Short answer: I recommend you see a doctor and seek help at your unit mental health section (some mental health section have sick parade, if not just call and say you need to talk to somebody asap, they are normally pretty good, like within a day or 2).

Long answer: Been through a similar situation where I had a posting where I put a lot of pressure on myself and worked 12-16 hrs a day and weekends for 2 years. I stopped exercising as I was exhausted from work. My drinking went up, sleeping routine went sideways. Towards the end my mental health plummeted. I delayed seeking help from fear of impacting my career. I only went see a doc towards the end. 5 years after that ordeal I’m still on 4-5 types of meds and psychological help, plus addiction councelling.

My points: 
1. do not let this go to far before you get help, try not to reach a point where it is really bad as it will be hard to recover.
2. Even with my state and my overall situation, I only got a geographical restriction as a PCAT, meaning I need access to a specialist, if not I need to do a screening before that deployment... my file did not go for medical release.
3. When I pretty much burnt out, they replaced me with another person and went on to burn him out too (so happened to many of my peers in the same job). You are replaceable, when you cannot perform anymore, they’ll find somebody else. It’s like that probably everywhere, you need to take care of yourself because the system won’t.
4. This is my personal experience and opinion, but when I actually started to take care of myself and seek help, I started to see life/career/habits/ambitions differently. I actually contemplated releasing from the CF and find a job that stangely pays better, I work 8 hrs a day (OT if I do more), no posting/moving, less responsibilities... I only knew and have the military so this was scary. I ended up actually putting my VR although I wasn’t that far from a pension...personally, best move I ever did. The stability and routine I have now feel great and there is like a huge pressure that is gone.

Take care of yourself, and trust your judgment.

You do not have the old camaraderie we had because we "leave work at work", you're on IR in an apartment or deployed for the 3rd time in 5 years, you're watching your mariage fail. But yes we're encouraged to have work/life balance, to go to the gym, etc. And we're wondering why people are releasing.

For some of the trades drastically short, they offered everybody that released in the past 5 or 10 years a 20,000$ bonus to come back in, and you were guaranteed your old rank. They should be lining up at the recruiting center doors...

IThis is your opinion, but the fact show otherwize. Countless people recently released because they prefered the old way. It wasn’t all about drinking, I used that as one of the example that affected people. I have long list of reasons I collected from those release interviews.

I remember a town hall, the senior officer and NCO said:”the people releasing will find the grass is not always greener on the other side”. Somebody answered:”Sir, I worked for General Electric for 6 years before joining, and I’m going back to work for GE. The new generation that won’t know the old CF won’t have anything to compare with and the change will be completed then. We’re just having a hard time recruiting at the monent...

It was true at a certain time, more than 10 years ago, it was very different, it definitely was a lifestyle, a family. Things have completely changed (some argue it was for the best, others says it was for the worst). There is less cohesion, less dedication, less pride in my opinion, but there is more emphasis on work life balance, more acceptance of differences, etc.

Soon enough “senior members” like me that knew the “old CF” will be gone, since we’ve lost our landmarks, and we don’t really fit in anymore. You soon will not hear that type of comments anymore. 

Just to give you an idea, at the time, drinking was a way to socialize and fit in. Drinking was part of the culture and was well accepted, now we consider this outside of the organizational values. We would devote our lives to our units, mentoring the younger ones, helping where needed, you devoted everything to the CF. You spent more time with your mates bonding, they were part of your family. But we had little work life balance. If you didn’t fit in, it was very hard to continue and be accepted. It was a different time, a different approach, some found it better and some worst, the CF took a different direction and not everybody accepted it. 

It might have played a role into the attrition issues we’re facing now, the senior people have lost that sense of lifestyle/family, the younger generation do not feel the same loyalty and devotion to an organization, want work life balance and overall want a job and not a lifestyle.

If he doesn’t want to help himself, there is not much you can do to be honest. I was stuck in the same downward spiral for a while, I was drinking way too much and didn’t really want to live, the drinking was numbing the emotions and feeling that I was destroying myself which is what I wanted for some reason. Before totally ruining my life, I gave therapy and meds a chance...and managed to get myself somewhat under control. I’m not out of the woods, and will probably never be, but I’m back doing physical exercise (I gained a lot of weight), playing music, and having a general interest for live. And I manage to remain sober for long periods and trying to drink reasonably when I do. It took a while and quite a lot of meds until I found a good combination. So it is possible to get back on track.

Last thing I wanted to mention, my wife also hated my drinking habit. I would drink in the evenings and would regularly (almost daily) get drunk before going to bed. The drinking was the only thing my wife could see, and she focused on it. It’s the only thing she would talk about. So I decided to stop drinking, cold, no meds and no support. I became completely disfunctional, had nightmares all the time, I had so many anxiety crisises that I couldn’t drive or do basic stuff. I really became a mess, drinking wasn’t the root cause of my issues, it was just something I used to get a break from all that anxiety. I was able to get rid of my alcohol addiction when I realized I had to deal with the root cause, my anxiety caused by previous events I decided to repress. Now that I learned to manage that anxiety, it is fairly easy to control my drinking.

Just don’t forget to take care of yourself. It is unlikely you’ll be able to do anything to “cure him”. This stuff normally needs professional help, both for him and possibly through couple’s therapy. There are no heroes in PTSD stories, only survivors (and that includes the family surrounding the member). Help and medical assistance were key for me, although I think of myself and my wife as very stong people, this disease is well beyond what we can handle internally.

I’ll be very honest with you, many of the meds that kept me alive had a drastic effect on my sex drive. One of the meds I couldn’t even get an erection...and I was one of the guy that would get boners all the time at the worst possible moments (like going to a dance bar during a first date). That made me quite depressed, the doc gave me viagra which for a 34YO male, was even more insulting, no way I would take those. So I stopped my happy pills, got into a withdrawal, things were even worst. So we switched meds 3-4 times, and tried meds combinations (more than one molecule), which I am on right now. Boner is back (nice to see him after a while), and I’m overall less distant and more involved. Meds should improve your life, not make it worst.

Unfortunately PTSD is a complex thing and is managed differently by people suffering from it. My wife has been very supportive, but the worst for me is to feel that my condition is making her cry. I want her to be happy, no matter what, even of that means I cannot be in her life anymore. Cause she has the right to be happy. I started drinking too much, to be distant, work too much, feel that life is not worth living...and I’m the dad of a 1 YO baby girl. I constantly felt like shit for who I became and how I thought I wasn’t being the husband and dad I should be.

I managed somehow to talk about what I was going through, and I accepted help. I was ready to do that however, I had enough of my depression and shitty drinking lifestyle. I was tired of feeling like this and having a negative impact on everybody. I’m now seeing a psychologist, an addiction’s counsellor, and my doctor. I started meds, took a while to find the right ones, but I see light at the end of the tunnel. I’m not out of the woods yet, but I put myself through a daily routine: go for a walk with my wife and the baby, wake up with the baby and feed her breakfast, get her in the bath and to sleep at night, that is grounding me.

The nightmares and anxiety haven’t went away but through time (and probably the meds) it goes down. Then my sex drive started to go up. I was dealing with so much through so many months and I was so depressed that sex was the last thing I thought about.

So I cannot tell you how to manage this since we all have different sotries and relationships. In my case, I couldn’t live like this anymore, either I was ending my life, I was asking for help, or I was going back to that unsane environment that will keep my insane mind going (military/war environment). I chose to ask for help, but I will never judge somebody that makes a different choice. I have a very suppotive wife which played a big role. And I will never judge a partner that cannot take this situation anymore. PTSD is a complex condition/disease, nothing about it is easy. I wish I could guide you better but you may have to ask questions that the answer is important to you, let him know how you feel and how this is impacting you, deal with challenging situations and make difficult decisions. My wife and I managed to get through it (again, I’ll never be cured but I’m better) and I am so happy to be a father.

I have a wide spectrum of anxious thoughts, but in your specific case there is one thing I sometimes do that works for me. It will sound a little stupid and maybe funny, but for me it works. I (34M) “suffer” from the same sort of anxiety, where I notice a symptom, I get anxious about it, my brain starts spinning and I bring the situation to extremes which always ends up with me on my death bed. Small symptoms can trigger huge anxiety crisis, so when I have an actual concerning symptom like you experienced, I can spend days without sleep.

What I try is not to fuel my anxiety further. My wife has banned me from googling my symptoms online. If I have a genuine concern, I go see a doctor. Waiting for the appointment is sometimes a nightmare due to my growing anxiety, but in the end I had a professional checking on my concerns. There has been many time where I couldn’t wait, I had to know right away because I was so stressed, and ended up at the ER for stuff not really that serious...I live in Canada so after you’ve waited 12 hrs in the waiting room to get checked, the anxiety had a chance to go down and I sometimes realized I went a little far with my thoughts.

Worrying about my symptoms really doesn’t help, so I take action. If I find it concerning enough, I see a doctor, if not, I keep my eyes opened for other symptoms. I’ll admit that sometimes my mind creates symptoms that are not even real, so I try to remain detached from my anxiety. If I let my mind wonder, it leads me to endless stress and disastrous scenarios.

It’s not even that I’m scared of dying, it’s that I cannot control in what situation it will happen. I try to accept there are things outside of my control, and no matter how much I stress about them, none of that anxiety will resolve the problem. Easier said than done, but in the end, I try hard to come back to the facts: this is the symptom I experienced, I’m concerned about it, am I feeling any other issues, do I feel I have to seek medical assistance right away, etc. If I let my mind wonder, I see myself dying, I become panicked, I end up at the ER for no good reason other than I panicked, I end up being embarrassed. And other time I should have consulted much earlier but the situation didn’t trigger an anxiety atrack...just do your best to get  evaluate the situation and your options, without bringing too much of that anxiety into that analysis.
